title: What happens when a multiple of four is added to another even number?
description: A multiple of four, written four p, is added to an even number that is not a multiple of four, written four q plus two. The sum is written with a bracket to show the rows and the two dots left over, then tried with three examples. The method is the same as the examples in the book on adding even numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: full rows of four join into more full rows, but the two dots left over never fill a row, so the sum is never a multiple of four. Watch for students who think any sum of two even numbers must be a multiple of four.

source: Pairs to Make Fours: the third case
video_script.why: A learner writes the sum of four p and four q plus two, sees that two dots are always left over, and checks with examples.
video_script.substitution: the book's own forms: four p and four q plus two
video_script.anchor: dots in rows of four, with the dots left over set apart, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: The sum is four times p plus q, plus two. It always leaves two over, so it is never a multiple of four.

final_answer.value: The sum is 4(p + q) + 2, so it always leaves a remainder of 2 and is never a multiple of 4
final_answer.spoken: the sum is four times p plus q, plus two, so it always leaves two over and is never a multiple of four

hold_back: The sum is 4(p + q) + 2, so it always leaves a remainder of 2 and is never a multiple of 4
maths_rules: 4(p + q) is full rows of four; the 2 left over dots cannot fill a row of four
like even + odd: the single left over cannot be paired
video_script.design: One idea: the full rows join and the two left over dots stay. Assumes the examples on the forms four p and four p plus two. The dot rows stay on the board with the two leftover dots set apart.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about adding two even numbers.
<bookmark mark='same'/>One is a multiple of four, and the other is not. We will solve it the same way as the examples in your book.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is the sum ever a multiple of four?

narration: <bookmark mark='left'/>A multiple of four is four p, which is p full rows of four.
<bookmark mark='right'/>An even number that is not a multiple of four is four q plus two. It is q full rows with two dots left over.

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers are four p and four q plus two, and we add them.

beats.on_screen: To find: what the sum looks like, and whether it is like even plus odd
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find what the sum looks like, and whether it is like even plus odd.

narration: <bookmark mark='join'/>Step one, join the two numbers. The brackets can go.
<bookmark mark='write'/>The sum is four p plus four q plus two.

marks.rows: the rows of both blocks stack into p plus q full rows

narration: <bookmark mark='rows'/>Step two, take out the four. Four p plus four q is four times p plus q.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The sum is four times p plus q, plus two.

beats.on_screen: p + q full rows of four, and 2 dots left over: never a full row. Like even + odd: the single left over cannot be paired

marks.full: the p plus q rows are full rows of four
marks.left: the two dots stay apart and cannot fill a row
marks.odd: an even plus odd picture with one single dot left appears beside it

narration: <bookmark mark='full'/>Step three, look at the rows. There are p plus q full rows, and two dots left over.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Two dots can never fill a row of four, so the sum is never a multiple of four.
<bookmark mark='odd'/>It is like even plus odd, where one single is left over and cannot be paired.

marks.first: four plus six shows ten, which is two rows and two over
marks.second: twelve plus eighteen shows thirty, which is seven rows and two over
marks.third: eight plus twenty two shows thirty, which is seven rows and two over

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step four, put examples back. Four plus six is ten, which is four times two, plus two.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Twelve plus eighteen is thirty, which is four times seven, plus two.
<bookmark mark='third'/>Eight plus twenty two is also thirty, four times seven, plus two. Every time, two are left over.
